extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, legislators, policymakers, and legal academics interested in statutory design and constitutional limits on delegation and veto powers
extracted.subtask_description: Design and evaluation of a statutory scheme (a 'Rulemaking Enabling Act') requiring congressional consideration of agency rulemakings and defining when administrative actions are 'legislative' for purposes of congressional veto power. The material addresses doctrinal tests, practical mechanics (timing/presentation), and comparative tradeoffs with alternatives like the REINS Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative veto constitutionality by act type
rubrics_metrics.description: A legislative veto of an executive or judicial act, for instance, could never be constitutional, but a legislative veto of a legislative act would be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes constitutionally permissible uses of a legislative veto (only over legislative acts) from impermissible uses (vetoing executive or judicial acts). Explains that veto-constitutionality inquiries turn on the nature of the vetoed act (legislative vs. executive/judicial) rather than on a categorical prohibition of congressional vetoes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of legislative power: defines boundaries of conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: An act of legislative power defines the boundary between permitted and forbidden conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses a Locke/Hamilton-inspired test: legislative power is the authority to make 'standing rules' so people know what is lawful. This definition supports identifying which agency actions are legislative and thus subject to congressional review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workable rule: rulemaking regulating private conduct is legislative
rubrics_metrics.description: Any rulemaking regulating private conduct on the part of an agency is legislative action because such rulemakings usually demarcate permissible and impermissible conduct for the first time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposes a pragmatic, slightly overinclusive bright-line: treat agency rulemakings that regulate private conduct as legislative. The Article acknowledges this rule may be marginally overinclusive but argues it is a substantial improvement on modern practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjudications that establish new principles prospectively are legislative
rubrics_metrics.description: Insofar as an adjudication establishes 'new principle[s]' to be applied prospectively, it can be considered legislative and subject to the veto of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizes agencies can try to make law via adjudication (Chenery II, Bell Aerospace). Where adjudication produces prospective rules affecting private rights, it should be treated like rulemaking and subject to congressional oversight; Congress should not permit adjudication to be used to evade review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vague license-criteria render determinations legislative
rubrics_metrics.description: When criteria are so vague as to provide no true guide to behavior—for example, when licenses shall issue if they are in the 'public interest'—then any act determining what is or is not permissible even in a particular case is legislative in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If statutory criteria leave enormous breadth of discretion, an individual determination effectively sets primary rules of conduct and thus should be treated as legislative power subject to congressional review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies must not use adjudication to evade congressional veto
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should not permit adjudications to replace rulemakings for the purpose of avoiding the congressional veto power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns against agency strategy of shifting substantive lawmaking into adjudication to avoid legislative review; cites NLRB practice and Chenery/Bell Aerospace authorities as contexts where line-drawing matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentment Clause requires Presidential assent for legislative rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive-administrative veto is required by the Constitution’s Presentment Clause. For any legislative rule to become law ... it requires the President’s assent. The President, like Congress, can give his assent through silence—and as such, much of the modern administrative state would operate undisturbed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any statutory design must account for presidential presentment: rules must be presented to the President; assent may be by inaction; disapproval triggers the usual presidential veto/override mechanics (two-thirds override). The Article emphasizes presentment constrains how congressional and executive roles interlock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional assent by inaction (default assent model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress and the President would assent by taking no action, or perhaps Congress would take no action and the President would enthusiastically take ownership of the newly enacted rulemaking. This model accepts that Congress can consent by taking no action and thereby accepts the validity of delegation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Rulemaking Enabling Act model treats congressional inaction as assent (default rule), differing from REINS (which requires affirmative congressional enactment). Political practicability is improved because most rules would become law by default unless Congress acts to disapprove.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must afford Congress opportunity to object or exceed statutory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Rulemaking Enabling Act ... the agency would not have authority to promulgate a rulemaking without affording Congress an opportunity to object. In other words, it is not Congress that would be exceeding its constitutional authority by vetoing the proposed rulemaking, but rather the agency that would be exceeding its statutory authority by exercising power without meeting the conditions of the delegation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory delegations should include procedural preconditions (transmission/notice to Congress). Failure to follow those conditions means the agency is acting outside its delegated authority—an enforceable limitation on agency power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed Rulemaking Enabling Act: timing & transmission requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Any agency ... shall transmit to the Congress not later than May 1 of the year in which a rule prescribed under section 553 ... is to become effective a copy of the proposed rule. Such rule shall take effect no earlier than December 1 of the year in which such rule is so transmitted unless otherwise provided by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets concrete calendar deadlines: transmission by May 1 and delayed effectiveness until December 1 (absent other law), giving Congress time to consider and act. Applies to independent commissions as well despite contrary governing statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation to the President and consequences of presidential inaction
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Congress enacts such rule, or an amended version of it, the rule ... shall be presented to the President ... before the same shall take effect, shall be approved by him, or being disapproved by him, shall be repassed by two thirds of the Senate and House of Representatives. If any such rule shall not be returned by the President within ten days after it shall have been presented to him, the same shall be a law, in like manner as if he had signed it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mirrors Article I, §7 presentment mechanics: president's signature or inaction produces law; disapproval triggers potential congressional override. Statutory draft explicitly folds presentment into the rulemaking-review regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating congressional/no-action and partial-house action rules
rubrics_metrics.description: If Congress takes no action in the allotted time, such inaction shall be construed as assent to the rule, but such rule must still be presented to the President ... If either house of Congress takes action on the rule but no final bill is enacted by the allotted time, Congress shall be construed to have taken no action and the rule shall become law. But if the full Congress enacts a resolution of disapproval, the rule shall not become law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies how to interpret different patterns of congressional behavior: default assent if no final disapproval; partial-house activity without a final enactment does not block the rule; only a full-Congress resolution of disapproval prevents the rule from taking effect (subject to presentation to President).

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional one-house veto language
rubrics_metrics.description: Optional provision: 'If the full Congress, or either the House or the Senate, enacts a resolution of disapproval, the rule shall not become law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft acknowledges an optional formulation that would permit a one-house veto. The choice between optional one-house veto language and stricter bicameralism involves doctrinal risk under Chadha and political tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: REINS Act vs. Rulemaking Enabling Act: default rule tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: The REINS Act ... would require all significant rulemakings to be passed by Congress and signed by the President before they became law. ... If the REINS Act were passed, many rulemakings would not become law because Congress could not muster the willpower to vote on them all. The Rulemaking Enabling Act, on the other hand, reverses this inertia: it accepts delegation to agencies and allows agency rules by default to become law. It is only when Congress affirmatively acts that those rulemakings may not become law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the practical and political differences: REINS imposes affirmative legislative burden (likely gridlock), while the Rulemaking Enabling Act preserves delegation and uses negative assent to permit governance to continue unless Congress disapproves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional choice to reserve different veto powers
rubrics_metrics.description: That act could reserve a one-house veto power, it could reserve only a bicameral veto power, or it could reserve a presidential veto power, or a combination of the presidential veto power with one of the first two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that statutory drafters can choose the institutional reservation: which actors get review/veto powers (one house, both houses, President) and in what combination; each choice has doctrinal and political implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold-of-discretion test for nondelegation concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: The nondelegation doctrine, after all, assumes that the breadth of discretion is what determines whether a statute unlawfully delegates legislative power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating delegations, focus on how much discretion is granted—statutes that provide no intelligible principle may violate nondelegation. This supports statutory designs that either limit discretion or provide review mechanisms (like congressional oversight) when discretion is broad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive-administrative veto likely to be rare in practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive-administrative veto might also seem jarring. It should not, however, for two reasons. First, such a veto would rarely be used ... As a general rule, this power would remain largely unused because Presidents still take significant ownership over administrative rulemakings promulgated during their own administrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance on expected use: political costs (charges of meddling, wasting resources) and presidential ownership of prior rulemakings mean an executive veto of agency-originated rules would be uncommon; the design can therefore include an executive veto without unduly disrupting governance.
